meta.blurb: Teo, forty-six, keeps forgetting names and where he put his keys. His friend Ada, a psychology teacher, gives him twelve rules about sleep, attention, memory and calm. Each one is simple, backed by real research and easy to try this week.
meta.bible: Teo: a cheerful, forgetful man of forty-six who works in an office and wants a sharper memory. Ada: his friend and neighbour, a psychology teacher, patient, funny and careful never to promise too much. Mia: Teo's niece, ten years old, who asks for explanations. They meet in Ada's kitchen on twelve Sunday evenings, one Rule each week. Hermann Ebbinghaus: a real German psychologist who studied forgetting in the 1880s. Key terms: Consolidation, Attention, Retrieval, Spacing, Forgetting curve, Cortisol, Hippocampus, Mediterranean, Plasticity, Memory palace. The twelve rules: Sleep, Move, One thing at a time, Spread it out, Test yourself, Calm the stress, Explain it, Feed it, People, Pictures and stories, Rest and wander, Stay curious. Facts: the brain is about two percent of body weight but uses about twenty percent of the body's energy at rest. Adults usually need about seven to nine hours of sleep. The World Health Organization advises about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. Voice: friendly, clear and honest; the science is real and hedged where the evidence is mixed; no invented numbers, studies or quotes. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: In one bad morning, Teo forgets a colleague's name, the code for his bank card and where he parked the car. He begins to wonder whether his brain is getting old.
Teo tells his friend Ada, who teaches psychology, about his bad day. She does not promise a miracle, but she offers him twelve rules, one for each Sunday evening.
Rule one, says Ada, is sleep. Teo admits that he has been sleeping about five hours a night for months and drinking too much coffee to get through the day.
While we sleep, the brain replays what happened during the day and helps to store the important parts. Scientists call this memory consolidation, and it works best when we get enough sleep.
A short night makes it harder to concentrate, to learn and to control our moods. Most adults need about seven to nine hours of sleep, although the right amount differs from person to person.
Ada suggests a regular bedtime, a cool dark bedroom, no screens in the last hour and no coffee after lunch. If sleep problems continue for weeks, she says, he should see a doctor.
The following Sunday, Ada announces rule two, which is to move. The brain is part of the body, she says, so what is good for the body is usually good for the brain.
When we exercise, the heart pumps harder and more blood reaches the brain. Many studies link regular activity with better memory, mood and attention, although the effects are usually modest.
Ada tells him that the World Health Organization advises about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week. A brisk walk before a hard task can also help him to feel more alert.
Ada is honest that exercise will not cure memory problems or guarantee a sharp mind in old age. It is simply one of the best habits we have, so Teo picks a sport he enjoys.
At work, Teo often answers emails while he is on a phone call. When he checks his work later, he finds that he has made several silly mistakes and has missed part of the call.
Ada says that attention is like a narrow spotlight that can only light one thing at a time. What we call multitasking is really switching the spotlight quickly from one task to another.
Each time we switch tasks, we lose a little time and make more mistakes. Studies of office workers suggest that after an interruption it can take many minutes to return fully to the original task.
Teo tries focused blocks of work. He silences his notifications, puts his phone in a drawer and works on one task for forty minutes before he checks anything else.
Teo is learning Italian for a holiday and crams for a class test the night before. He passes, but a week later he has forgotten most of the words.
Ada tells him about Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist who studied his own forgetting in the 1880s. He found that new memories fade quickly at first and then more slowly.
The cure is spacing. If you review something after a day, then a few days, then a week and then a month, each review makes the memory last longer.
Teo changes his plan and studies Italian for ten minutes on most days instead of for two hours once a week. He puts review dates on his calendar so that he never has to remember them.
Teo likes to read his notes again and again, and each time they seem more familiar. He feels sure that he knows the material, until a friend asks him a simple question and his mind goes blank.
When we reread, the words start to feel familiar, and we mistake this feeling for knowledge. Recognising something on a page is much easier than recalling it from memory.
The better method is retrieval practice. Teo closes the book, writes down everything he can remember, and then checks his notes, and the effort of pulling the facts out makes the memory stronger.
Making mistakes during practice is not a failure. When Teo checks the right answer and tries again later, the correction often sticks better than a fact he never got wrong.
Before an important presentation, Teo's heart pounds and his palms are damp. Then, standing in front of the room, he forgets the first slide completely.
In small amounts, stress can be useful, because the body releases hormones such as cortisol that make us more alert. The trouble begins when the stress is too strong for the moment.
Long stress is different, because it can wear us down. Studies link stress that lasts for months with trouble with memory and mood, although scientists are still working out exactly how.
Ada teaches him slow breathing, in for four counts and out for six, and she also recommends walks, talking to friends and real breaks. If worry is constant, she says, a doctor can help.
Teo's ten-year-old niece Mia asks him how the gears on her bicycle work. He has ridden bikes all his life, yet he finds that he cannot explain it properly.
To explain something, you have to put the ideas in order, and the gaps become obvious. That is why trying to explain a topic is such a powerful way to learn it.
Ada suggests explaining a topic out loud in plain words, to a friend, a child or even an empty chair. Wherever he stumbles, that is the part he needs to study again.
When Teo finally explains the gears to Mia, she asks sharp questions that make him think harder. Teaching her has taught him more than any book could.
Teo skips lunch for a meeting, and by three in the afternoon he feels foggy and irritable. Ada says this is rule eight, which is to feed the brain properly.
The brain makes up only about two percent of our weight, yet it uses about twenty percent of the body's energy. That is a lot of fuel for an organ that never rests.
Regular meals and enough water help the brain to work well. Some studies suggest that even mild dehydration can make it harder to concentrate, so Teo puts a bottle on his desk.

Some studies link Mediterranean-style eating, with lots of vegetables, beans, fish and olive oil, with better brain health. No single food will fix a memory, however, and heavy drinking is clearly harmful.
Teo goes to dinner with five friends he has not seen for a year. He laughs a lot, and the next day he feels sharper and happier than he has in weeks.
A good conversation is a real workout for the brain. We have to listen, remember, understand what the other person means and decide what to say, all within seconds.
Studies link long-term loneliness with poorer health and a higher risk of memory problems. It is hard to know which causes which, but staying connected is clearly a good thing for most people.
Ada tells him to make friendship a habit. Teo joins a choir on Wednesday evenings, phones one friend every week and begins to say yes to invitations that he used to refuse.
At the supermarket Teo forgets half of his shopping, yet he can describe the whole plot of a film he saw last month. Ada says this is a clue for rule ten.
People generally remember pictures better than words. Scientists call this the picture superiority effect, and it means that turning a fact into a clear image can help us to remember it.
A story links facts together so that each one leads to the next. Ancient Greek and Roman speakers used a related trick, the memory palace, to remember long speeches.

To try it, Teo imagines walking through his own home and puts one item from his list in each room. He imagines a loaf of bread on the sofa and an egg in the bath, and when he needs the list, he walks through again.
Teo has been stuck on a work problem for hours. He gives up and walks to the shop, and halfway there the answer suddenly comes to him.
Attention is like a muscle that gets tired when it is used for a long time. Short breaks, perhaps five minutes every hour, seem to help people to concentrate again.
When the mind wanders, it connects ideas and makes plans in the background. This means that moments of boredom or daydreaming are not wasted time but a useful kind of thinking.
One small study found that people who walked came up with more creative ideas than people who sat. Sleep also helps, which is why a hard problem often looks easier after a night's rest.
The last rule is to stay curious. The brain changes with experience at every age, a quality that scientists call plasticity, so learning something new and difficult keeps it flexible.
Ada clears away some myths. We use all of our brain and not just ten percent, and there is little evidence for fixed learning styles or for brain games that make you smarter in daily life.
Twelve weeks later, Teo feels very different. He sleeps better, walks every day, uses spaced notes and remembers the names of his colleagues, and he knows that small habits work best together.
Teo's story is meant to inform, not to treat. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so if you worry about your memory, please talk to a doctor.
C1C2: In the space of a single bad morning, Teo forgot the name of a colleague he had known for years, the number of his own bank card and the street where he had left his car. By lunchtime a small, cold worry had settled in his mind, and he wondered whether this was the beginning of something serious. It did not occur to him that the problem might be more ordinary, and far more fixable.

That evening Teo poured out his worries to Ada, a psychology teacher who lived next door and who had a reputation for never overpromising. She told him that the brain is not a machine that simply wears out, but a living organ that responds to the way it is treated, and that the research gave her twelve useful rules. There would be no pills, tricks or miracles, she warned him, only habits that anyone could try.

Rule one, said Ada, was sleep, and she raised an eyebrow when Teo admitted that he had been getting about five hours a night for months. He had been relying on coffee, he confessed, to push through the long afternoons at his desk. A foggy mind, she told him, is often the simplest and most overlooked explanation for a forgetful one.

Sleep is not a switching off of the brain, Ada explained, but a busy period of housekeeping in which the day's experiences are replayed, sorted and stored. Scientists call this process memory consolidation, and studies suggest that it depends on getting enough of the right kind of sleep. Someone who learns something new and then sleeps well will usually remember it better than someone who stays awake.

A short night, Ada said, dulls attention, spoils mood and makes it far harder to take in new information. Most adults seem to need about seven to nine hours of sleep, although individuals differ, and many people who think they cope on less are in fact performing below their best. The tricky part is that tired people are poor judges of how tired they are.

Ada's advice was practical and unglamorous: go to bed and wake up at roughly the same time every day, keep the bedroom cool and dark, put the phone to charge in another room and avoid coffee after lunch. Within a week, she promised, he should notice some difference, although she added that long-lasting sleep problems deserve a doctor's attention and not just a new routine. Teo went home and, for once, turned off the television.

The following Sunday they walked along the river, because Ada said that rule two was best explained in motion. The brain is part of the body, she pointed out, and it depends on the same blood supply, so what is good for the heart and muscles is usually good for the mind as well. Teo, who had not walked anywhere in months, was surprised at how pleasant it felt.

When we exercise, the heart pumps harder and more oxygen-rich blood reaches the brain, and over time regular activity may help the brain to maintain itself. Many studies link exercise with better mood, attention and memory, and some suggest it may protect a region called the hippocampus, which is important for forming memories. Ada was careful to say that the effects are usually modest and that scientists are still working out the details.

A good target, Ada said, is the one suggested by the World Health Organization, which advises about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, such as brisk walking, cycling or swimming. Even a short burst can help in the moment, and many people find that a ten-minute walk before a difficult task leaves them feeling more alert. The best exercise, she added with a smile, is the one you will actually do.

Ada was careful not to oversell it, for exercise is no cure for forgetfulness and no guarantee of a sharp mind at eighty. It is simply one of the best habits that science has found, with a wide range of benefits for the body and the brain, and the habit lasts longest when it is enjoyable. Teo, who had loved football as a boy, joined a casual Thursday kickabout and found himself laughing again.

At work, Teo prided himself on being able to answer emails, follow a video call and send messages all at once. When he reread his work that evening, he found a string of silly errors, and he realised that he could not remember what had been agreed on the call. Ada nodded when he told her, for rule three, she said, was about exactly this: do one thing at a time.

Attention, Ada told him, behaves like a narrow spotlight that can illuminate only one thing clearly at a time. What we call multitasking is really rapid switching, in which the beam jumps from task to task while the brain struggles to reload each one. Only very familiar, automatic activities, such as walking while listening to music, can be done together without any real cost.

Every switch has a price, Ada said, because the brain needs a moment to put away one task and pick up the next, and in that gap mistakes slip in. Studies of office workers suggest that after an interruption it can take many minutes to return fully to what you were doing, which means that a busy day of pings and alerts can leave little time for real thought. Teo winced, since his phone buzzed fifty times a day.

Teo decided to experiment with focused blocks, and on Monday morning he silenced his notifications, put the phone in a drawer and gave one task forty uninterrupted minutes. To his surprise, the report that normally took him a whole afternoon was finished before lunch, and it contained far fewer mistakes. Ada was not surprised at all, for the principle had been known to scientists for decades.

Teo had signed up for an Italian evening class before a holiday, and the night before the first test he stayed up until two in the morning memorising word lists. He passed the test, but a week later, standing in a cafe in Rome, he could barely remember how to order a coffee. Rule four, said Ada, was written for people exactly like him.

More than a century ago, Ada told him, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory by learning lists of meaningless syllables and checking how many he still knew after various delays. He found that forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down, a pattern now known as the forgetting curve. The experiment has been repeated many times since, and its basic message holds up well.

The remedy, Ada explained, is spacing, which simply means returning to the material at widening intervals: after a day, after a few days, after a week, after a month. Each review arrives just as the memory begins to fade, and so it strengthens the trace and pushes the next forgetting further away. Studies of students have repeatedly found that spaced study beats cramming for lasting memory, even when the total time is the same.

Teo abandoned his marathon sessions and began studying Italian for ten minutes on most days, marking review dates on his calendar so that he never had to remember when to return. It felt almost too light to work, but after a month he was understanding whole sentences on the radio. Little and often, he decided, was a far more comfortable way to learn than a heroic effort once a week.

Teo's favourite way of studying had always been to reread his notes and highlight the important lines, and each pass left him more confident. Then a friend asked him a simple question about the subject over dinner, and his mind went completely blank. It was an uncomfortable moment, and Ada said it was a very common one, because rule five is about the difference between recognising something and truly knowing it.

When we reread a text, Ada said, the words begin to feel familiar, and the brain happily mistakes that comfortable feeling for real knowledge. Recognising something on a page is far easier than producing it from memory, and so rereading can create an illusion of learning that collapses when the page is taken away. It is the learner's equivalent of believing you can swim because you have watched other people do it.

The better method, Ada said, is retrieval practice, which means closing the book and trying to bring the information back out of your own head, using a blank page, a set of flashcards or a quiz. The effort of retrieval is not a sign that something has gone wrong, because that very struggle is what strengthens the memory and makes it easier to find next time. Research on this so-called testing effect is among the most solid in the whole field.

Ada urged him not to be afraid of wrong answers during practice, for a mistake that is quickly corrected is one of the most effective teachers there is. When you check the right answer and then try again after a gap, the correction frequently sticks better than a fact you never got wrong. Teo started to enjoy his flashcard sessions, and he began to think of every error as a small gift.

On the morning of an important presentation, Teo's heart was pounding, his palms were damp and his mouth felt like sandpaper. Then, standing in front of twenty colleagues, he completely lost the opening of his talk and stood in silence for what felt like a week. That evening Ada told him that rule six was about stress, and that his reaction was neither weakness nor strange.

A little stress is not the enemy, Ada said, for in short bursts the body releases hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline that make us more alert and ready to act. Performance tends to rise with a moderate level of arousal and then fall again when the pressure becomes overwhelming, which is probably what happened to Teo at the front of the room. The skill, then, is not to remove stress but to keep it in a useful range.

Chronic stress, Ada warned, is a different matter, because stress that goes on for months keeps the body in a state of alarm and appears to wear on the brain. Studies link long-lasting stress with poorer memory, lower mood and difficulty concentrating, although scientists are still debating exactly how the effects arise. It was no wonder, she added gently, that a man working long hours and sleeping five of them was struggling to remember things.

Ada taught him a simple tool: breathe in slowly for a count of four and out for a count of six, and repeat it for a minute or two, which tends to settle the body's alarm system. Walks, honest conversations with friends and genuine breaks from work all help as well, she said. She added that constant, overwhelming worry is not something to tough out alone, and that a doctor can offer real support.

One afternoon Teo's ten-year-old niece Mia asked him how the gears on her bicycle worked, and he opened his mouth to answer before realising that he had no idea. He had been riding bicycles for forty years and had always felt that he understood them, yet the moment he tried to put it into words the picture fell apart. Rule seven, Ada said that evening, was hiding in that very experience.

To explain something clearly, Ada said, you have to put the ideas in order, choose examples and notice which links are missing, and in doing so you discover exactly where your understanding is thin. This is why trying to explain a subject is one of the most powerful ways to learn it, and why teachers so often say that they learned most when they taught. A feeling of understanding, it turns out, is not the same as understanding itself.

Ada's method was wonderfully simple: choose a topic, explain it out loud in plain words as if to a curious child, and notice where you stumble, hesitate or reach for jargon. Those are the places where your knowledge is thin, and you can go back to the book, fix them, and try again. Teo practised on a kitchen chair for two evenings and, by Sunday, he could explain bicycle gears to Mia in three minutes flat.

When Teo finally explained the gears to Mia, drawing two cogs of different sizes on a sheet of paper, she asked sharp questions that made him think harder than he had in months. Teaching her, he discovered, had taught him more than another hour with a textbook ever could, and the next time he rode a bicycle he saw the machine in a completely new light. He also noticed, with pleasure, that Mia had not forgotten a word of it.

On a day when meetings swallowed his lunch hour, Teo found by three o'clock that he could not read a simple paragraph without losing the thread, and he snapped at a colleague for no reason. Ada listened with a knowing smile and announced rule eight, which was to feed the brain properly. It is an organ that cannot store much fuel and depends on a steady supply.

The brain accounts for only about two percent of body weight, Ada said, yet it consumes roughly twenty percent of the energy the body uses at rest, which makes it an expensive organ to run. Its supply of fuel arrives continuously through the blood, and an irregular or poor diet can show up quickly in mood, concentration and patience. There is no need for panic, she added, since the body is good at keeping the supply steady when we eat regularly.

Regular meals help to keep blood sugar steady, Ada said, and enough water matters as well, because some studies suggest that even mild dehydration can reduce attention and make people feel tired and irritable. The evidence is not perfect, and needs differ from person to person, but a bottle of water on the desk is cheap and harmless. Teo promised to eat lunch every day and to stop treating his coffee as a meal.

Researchers have found that people who eat in a Mediterranean style, with plenty of vegetables, beans, fish, nuts and olive oil, tend to have better brain health as they age. These studies show associations and not proof, Ada pointed out, and no single superfood will repair a memory, whatever the headlines may say. Heavy drinking, by contrast, is clearly harmful to the brain, and she suggested that Teo keep his own habits modest.

Teo spent Saturday evening at a long table with five old friends he had not seen for a year, and the conversation lasted until the restaurant began stacking the chairs. The next morning he felt lighter and sharper than he had in weeks, and when he told Ada, she smiled and said that it was a perfect illustration of rule nine. People, she said, are good for the brain.

A good conversation, Ada said, is a remarkable workout for the brain, because we have to listen closely, hold what has been said in memory, read tone and expression, and prepare a reply, all within a few seconds. Few activities draw so many mental skills together, and it happens to be one that most people enjoy. The brain, it seems, is built for company in a way that it is not built for solitary struggle.

Many studies have found that long-term loneliness is linked with poorer health and a greater risk of memory difficulties later in life, though it is difficult to separate cause from effect. A lonely person may also sleep badly, move less and feel low, and each of those habits can affect the mind. Whatever the exact mechanism, Ada said, staying connected is one of the kindest things you can do for your brain.

Ada urged him to treat friendship as a habit rather than a happy accident, because people tend to drift apart unless someone makes an effort. Teo joined a community choir on Wednesday evenings, committed to phoning one old friend each week, and began to say yes to invitations that he would once have turned down. His calendar became fuller, his evenings warmer and, to his surprise, his memory sharper.

At the supermarket Teo forgot half of what his sister had asked him to buy, yet on the way home he could describe every twist in a film that he had seen a month earlier. He told Ada about it that Sunday, half laughing at himself, and she said that the contrast was a clue to rule ten. Our memories, she explained, prefer pictures and stories to lists and numbers.

People tend to remember pictures far better than words, Ada said, and the finding is so reliable that psychologists have given it a name, the picture superiority effect. A vivid, unusual image seems to give the brain more to hold on to than a plain word does, which is why turning a dry fact into a picture can make it much easier to recall. The stranger or funnier the image, she added, the better it usually sticks.

A story ties separate facts into a chain, so that each item leads naturally to the next, and that is why we recall plots so much more easily than lists. Speakers in ancient Greece and Rome are said to have used a related technique, often called the memory palace, to remember long speeches without notes. It remains one of the best-known memory methods, and modern memory competitors still rely on it.

To try the method, Teo imagined walking slowly through his own flat and placed one item from his shopping list in each room, making each image as absurd as possible. A loaf of bread slept on the sofa, a giant egg floated in the bath, and a cheerful carrot waved from the bedroom window. When he returned to the supermarket, he took the same mental stroll and was astonished to bring back every single item.

For hours Teo had been wrestling with a scheduling problem at work, and the harder he tried, the more tightly it seemed to be knotted. In frustration he gave up and walked to the shop for a sandwich, and halfway along the street the solution arrived in his mind, complete and obvious. Rule eleven, Ada told him on Sunday, is to rest and let the mind wander.

Attention, Ada explained, is a limited resource that tires with use, and the mind is rarely at its best after long, unbroken stretches of effort. Short breaks, perhaps five or ten minutes every hour or so, seem to help people recover their focus, although the ideal rhythm varies between people and tasks. The important thing is that a break should be a real one, without a screen, and not just a different kind of work.

When the mind is allowed to wander, Ada said, it does not simply switch off, but links old memories and ideas, imagines the future and often stumbles on solutions that effortful thinking could not find. This means that moments of boredom, daydreaming or staring out of a train window are not wasted time but a quiet kind of work. Modern life, with a screen for every empty minute, leaves very little room for it.

One small study found that people who walked came up with more creative ideas than people who stayed seated, though more research is needed before anyone can promise results. Sleep also seems to help, which is why a hard problem so often looks simpler the next morning, and why Ada recommended keeping a notebook within reach. Teo began to take a short walk whenever he was stuck, and his ideas came more freely.

The last rule, Ada said, was perhaps the most hopeful, since it was to stay curious. The brain keeps changing in response to experience at every age, a quality that scientists call plasticity, and learning something new and genuinely difficult, such as an instrument, a language or a craft, keeps it flexible. Teo, who had already started Italian, bought a second-hand guitar that very weekend.

Ada also cleared away a few popular myths, which she said were worth knowing because they waste so much time and money. We use all of our brain and not merely ten percent, the idea of being strictly left-brained or right-brained is a distortion, and there is little good evidence for fixed learning styles. Brain-training games make people better at the games themselves, but they have not been shown to make people smarter in everyday life.

Twelve Sundays later, Teo laid the twelve cards in a row and realised how much had changed since that bad morning. He slept properly, walked every day, worked in focused blocks, reviewed his Italian at spaced intervals, sang on Wednesdays and could greet every colleague by name. None of the rules was dramatic on its own, but together they had turned a worried man into a confident one.

As the light faded over the porch, Teo and Ada drank a last cup of tea to twelve rules that had turned out to be mostly common sense, supported by good science. This book is general information and is not medical advice, and it cannot replace a doctor who knows your own situation, so anyone who is seriously worried about their memory should seek professional help without delay. For everyone else, the invitation is simple: pick one rule, try it this week, and see what your brain can do.
